description: We are a group of guys from Czechia looking for a challenge and some nice hands on practice.
summary:
We developed the Astronaut Health Monitor, an easy to use web app to help the astronaut track their own health and physical readiness during flight.

To deal with the issues of microgravity and deep space we have a very straightforward, intuitive graphical interface which brings all the key metrics together in one place. The crew do their daily check-ins (sleep, mood, symptoms, food, exercise) plus the 3 day physiological scans (BP, HR, temp, blood glucose, body mass, vision) plus the cabin sensors (radiation, CO2, temp). All the readings are compared against the individual astronaut's own baseline, the fitness equipment loads are automatically adjusted to the day's level of fatigue and we have a very friendly in-app assistant (our project mascot) to walk you through the step by step instructions for taking the microgravity measurements.

This is absolutely critical as astronauts out there are not going to be able to count on immediate outside assistance. The whole point of the Astronaut Health Monitor is to keep health monitoring as simple and understandable as possible so that the crew can look out for early warning signs and look after their own health.
details:
How It Works: We created a simple, interactive health dashboard so astronauts can check their status in seconds. Instead of digging through complicated medical charts, crew members look at a clean, black-and-white body map—with separate silhouettes for men and women—that tracks 12 key health and environment metrics like heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, sleep, mood, and radiation. Everything uses straightforward green, orange, and red color coding. Clicking any area brings up plain-English steps on how to take the measurement, why it matters in space, and what to do right away if a reading goes into the red.

Benefits & Impact: On deep-space missions to the Moon or Mars, crews face communication delays with Earth—and most astronauts aren't doctors. Our tool takes the panic and guesswork out of stressful moments by turning raw numbers into clear, step-by-step advice before a small issue turns into an emergency. Back on Earth, the exact same visual guide could help people in remote communities or disaster zones check their health when a doctor isn't around.

Tools & Data: We built the web app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using JSON datasets to simulate a 20-day mission for a four-person crew (M1 , M2 , F1 , F2). We modeled our numbers on real research from NASA’s Human Research Program and Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

Creativity & Factors Considered: We designed everything around human factors—asking ourselves how a tired or stressed crewmate would actually use this tool during a real crisis. We shaped the app around NASA’s five main hazards of spaceflight (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and closed environments), included separate male and female crew profiles, and adapted tracking across four mission settings: a spacecraft, space station, lunar base, and rover.
